citations.quote: Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so $\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. For $z\in\mathbb C$, define $$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$ whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of [[def-complex-integer-powers]] and [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
The complex exponential is entire, and $$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$, $$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$ Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with $$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$ Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex numbers** by the quotient ring $$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$ ([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set $$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$ Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map $\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of [[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]]. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a **limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$ The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. **The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so $$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$ and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So $q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the **derivative of $f$ at $c$** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$ **Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.** 1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]]

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$ **Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything (the sign function); both witnesses are on the companion page. **No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form: the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). **The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is continuous at every point of $S$. **No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the companion page.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$. Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: Write $w_j=\alpha_j+i\beta_j$ with $\alpha_j=\operatorname{Re}w_j$, $\beta_j=\operatorname{Im}w_j$ real and fix the component index $j$; by [F1] $e^{-i\omega t}=\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t$, so the product rule of [F2] with $(a,b)=(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ and $(c,s)=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t)$ gives $z_{p,j}(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w_j\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t)$ for every real $t$. The maps $t\mapsto\omega t$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ are smooth, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F3] give the derivatives of finite combinations, so each $z_{p,j}$ is $C^\infty$ and hence $z_p$ is $C^\infty$ by [F7].

Differentiating the display of step 1.1 componentwise with the rules of [F3] gives $z_{p,j}'(t)=\omega^{-1}(\alpha_j\sin\omega t-\beta_j\cos\omega t)$ and $z_{p,j}''(t)=\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t=\operatorname{Re}((\alpha_j+i\beta_j)(\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t))=\operatorname{Re}(w_je^{-i\omega t})$ for every $j$ and every real $t$, the middle equality by the product rule of [F2] and the last by [F1]; hence $z_p''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise.

Since $\omega(t+T)=\omega t+2\pi$, the display of step 1.1 and the period formulas $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$, $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ of [F4] give $z_{p,j}(t+T)=z_{p,j}(t)$ for every $j$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, so $z_p$ is $T$-periodic; with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this is claim (a).

Let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $\mathbb R$ and set $h:=z-z_p$; by step 2.1, $h''=0$ on $\mathbb R$. Fix $j$; the component $h_j$ is $C^2$, so $h_j'$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R$, which is the interior of $\mathbb R$ by [F5], with $(h_j')'=h_j''=0$; [F5] applied on the order-convex interval $\mathbb R$ therefore makes $h_j'$ a constant $b_j\in\mathbb R$. The map $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point with derivative $h_j'-b_j=0$, the derivative of $b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ being $b_j$ by [F3]; [F5] makes $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ a constant $a_j$, so $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ and $z=z_p+a+bt$ with $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$, $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$. If also $z=z_p+a'+b't$ on $\mathbb R$, evaluating at $t=0$ gives $a=a'$ and then differentiating at $t=0$ gives $b=b'$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique; this is claim (b).

Let $z=z_p+a+bt$ be a solution as in step 3.1. If $b=0$, then $z=z_p+a$ is $T$-periodic by step 2.2. Conversely, if $z$ is $T$-periodic, then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ together with $z_p(t+T)=z_p(t)$ of step 2.2 gives $b(t+T)=bt$, hence $bT=0$ and $b=0$ because $T>0$. The $T$-periodic solutions are therefore exactly the maps $z_p+a$ with $a\in\mathbb R^n$; their oscillating part is $z_p$ itself, whose defining formula $z_p(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$ exhibits the complex amplitude vector $-w/\omega^2$; this is claim (c).

Let $I$ be a nonempty open interval, $t_*\in I$, and let $z:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $I$; put $h:=z-z_p$ on $I$. Fixing $j$ and repeating the argument of step 3.1 on the order-convex interval $I$, every interior point of which lies in $I$ where the assumed derivatives exist, gives a constant $b_j$ on $I$ equal to $h_j'$, then a constant $a_j$ with $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ on $I$; hence $z=z_p+a+bt$ on $I$. Evaluating at $t_*$ gives $b=z'(t_*)-z_p'(t_*)$ and $a=z(t_*)-z_p(t_*)-bt_*$, and conversely those values reproduce $z$ on $I$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique. Define $Z(t):=z_p(t)+a+bt$ for all real $t$ with these $(a,b)$; by steps 2.1 and 2.2, $Z$ is a $C^\infty$ solution on $\mathbb R$ extending $z$. If $\tilde Z$ is any global $C^2$ solution on $\mathbb R$ agreeing with $z$ on $I$, then step 3.1 writes $\tilde Z=z_p+\tilde a+\tilde bt$ with a unique pair $(\tilde a,\tilde b)$; restricting to $I$ and using the uniqueness just proved gives $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$, so $\tilde Z=Z$ and the extension is unique.

For $Z$ as in step 4.2, step 4.1 gives that $Z$ is $T$-periodic if and only if $b=0$, which by step 4.2 is equivalent to $z'(t_*)=z_p'(t_*)$. If $t$ and $t+T$ both lie in $I$, then $Z(t+T)-Z(t)=bT$ while $Z$ agrees with $z$ at those two arguments, so equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ forces $bT=0$ and $b=0$. If $I$ contains no such pair, then the condition "$z(t+T)=z(t)$ whenever both $t$ and $t+T$ lie in $I$" has empty scope and is satisfied vacuously; the extension with any fixed nonzero $b$ obeys it and is not $T$-periodic, so the condition determines nothing about periodicity of the global extension.

Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and a component index $j$ and define $G_j(s):=-\omega^{-3}(\alpha_j\sin\omega s-\beta_j\cos\omega s)$ for $s\in[t,t+T]$; by the rules of [F3], $G_j$ is differentiable at every point of $[t,t+T]$ with $G_j'(s)=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega s+\beta_j\sin\omega s)=z_{p,j}(s)$. The map $z_{p,j}$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, hence continuous on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6], hence Riemann integrable on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6]; the fundamental theorem [F6] therefore gives $\int_t^{t+T}z_{p,j}=\omega^{-3}[\beta_j(\cos(\omega(t+T))-\cos\omega t)-\alpha_j(\sin(\omega(t+T))-\sin\omega t)]=0$, the vanishing because $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$ and $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ by [F4] and $\omega T=2\pi$. Summing over $j$ and dividing by $T$ gives mean zero for $z_p$ over $[t,t+T]$. For the affine part put $P(s):=as+bs^2/2$, differentiable with $P'(s)=a+bs$ by [F3]; the same fundamental theorem, the integrand $s\mapsto a+bs$ being continuous, gives $\frac1T\int_t^{t+T}(a+bs)\,ds=\frac{P(t+T)-P(t)}T=a+\frac{b((t+T)^2-t^2)}{2T}=a+b(t+\frac T2)$. Adding the two computations, the mean of $Z$ over $[t,t+T]$ is $a+b(t+T/2)$ for every real $t$, and it equals $a$ for every $t$ exactly when $b=0$, which by step 5.1 is exactly the periodicity condition; then the mean over every complete period is $a$. This completes the proof of (d) and of the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 4.2 and 5.1 distinguish the nonempty open solution interval from the possibly empty set of pairs t,t+T in I. When that pair set is empty the local periodicity test is vacuous; the unique global extension still has its classified affine drift.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show w=0 gives z_p identically zero, and steps 3.1 and 4.1 keep the zero drift b=0 as the periodic branch; step 6.1 computes the period mean a, which may be the zero vector. The zero-frequency value is excluded by omega>0.

Step 2.2 verifies periodicity at the single shift T; step 4.1 decides periodicity by the single equation bT=0; step 5.1 uses one admissible pair t and t+T in I; the n=1 component case is covered by the fixed component index j in steps 1.1 to 2.1.

boundaries.reason: Clause (d) quantifies only over nonempty open intervals, so a degenerate interval (a single point) is outside the hypothesis; the degenerate drift case b=0 is the periodic case treated in steps 4.1 and 5.1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 differentiates the difference h on all of R and step 6.1 integrates G_j on the closed interval from t to t+T with the fundamental theorem, G_j being continuous to the endpoints; step 5.1 evaluates the periodic equality only at pairs t and t+T that both lie in I.

The proof fixes finitely many component indices, times and the single point t_*, and applies the explicit derivative, integral and zero-derivative suppliers; the Statement declares no choice principle and step 4.2 uses only Corollary [F5].
Step 4.1: if a solution z_p+a+bt is T-periodic then b(t+T)=bt for every t, hence b=0; step 5.1 transfers the conclusion to the unique global extension Z.

Step 4.1 proves b=0 implies T-periodicity; step 5.1 transfers this to the unique global extension. By step 4.2 the condition is z-prime(t_*)=z_p-prime(t_*); no equality of the positions is required because the constant mean a is arbitrary.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$. $f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$ $f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of $X$. **The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$ and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$ Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice. **Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are always written out. **Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Then: 1. **The projections are continuous**, and the product topology is the coarsest topology on $P$ making all of them continuous. 2. **Characteristic property.** For every space $Z$ and every function $h : Z \to P$, $$h \text{ is continuous } \iff \pi_i \circ h \text{ is continuous for every } i \in I .$$ The functions $\pi_i \circ h$ are the **components** of $h$, and every family of functions $h_i : Z \to X_i$ arises from exactly one $h$, namely $h(z)(i) := h_i(z)$. 3. **The projections are open maps** ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]), for the product topology and for the box topology alike. They need not be closed; that failure is recorded on this page as a false statement. 4. **Surjectivity.** If every $X_i$ is nonempty then every $\pi_j$ is surjective. For $I$ a natural number this is a theorem of ZF ([[lem-finite-choice]]); for an arbitrary $I$ it is the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), and this is the only place in the item where a choice principle is used.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite $f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$. **No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly *continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over $0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then $f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous real-valued maps.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is continuous at every point of $S$. **No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the companion page.

If $w:D\to\mathbb C^3$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)$, applying the preceding conclusion at each fixed $x\in D$ gives $w(x)=0$ for every $x$, so $w\equiv0$; no continuity of $w$ is needed for this conclusion.

derivations.claim: [Setting and existence of the scattered field] The hypotheses of [F1] are met by the geometry, $k$ and $R$, and $e_T$ is a smooth $\mathbb C$-valued tangential field on $\partial O$ by [F7] applied to the $C^\infty$ incident field; hence [F1] supplies a unique $\widetilde E_{\rm scat}\in C^\infty(\overline D;\mathbb C^3)$ with $(\Delta+k^2)\widetilde E_{\rm scat}=0$, $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E_{\rm scat}=0$ on $D$, tangential trace $e_T$ on $\partial O$, and the outgoing modal condition on $S_R$. [Uniqueness of the outgoing scattered correction] Let $(\widetilde E',\widetilde B')$ be a $C^\infty$ frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on an open $V'\supseteq\overline D$, outgoing on $S_R$ in the modal sense of [F1], with tangential trace $e_T$ on $\partial O$. From the phasor equations and [F6], $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E'=i\omega\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B'=i\omega(-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E')=\omega^2c^{-2}\widetilde E'=k^2\widetilde E'$ and $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E'=0$, so [F6] gives $\nabla\operatorname{div}\widetilde E'-\Delta\widetilde E'=-\Delta\widetilde E'=k^2\widetilde E'$, that is $(\Delta+k^2)\widetilde E'=0$ on $D$. derivations.claim: [Off-support regularity and the Helmholtz equation] Since $S$ is compact and contained in the closed ball of radius $a$, choose the open ball $B_A(0)$ with $A:=a+1$, so that $S\subset B_A(0)$ and $\alpha$ is a finite complex measure supported in that open ball. By [F2] the field $G_k*\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ outside the support of $\alpha$ and solves $(\Delta+k^2)w=0$ there; since the support of $\alpha$ is contained in $S$, the field $u$ of [F1] is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there; the half-space $\{x_3>0\}$ is disjoint from the plane containing $S$, hence is contained in $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$, so $u$ is $C^\infty$ there as well.

[Elementary bounds: phase, radial expansion, kernel residual] First, for every real $\theta$ one has $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$: by [F6], $2(1-\cos\theta)=|e^{i\theta}-1|^2$ and $|\cos\theta|\le1$, and the Taylor bound for $\cos$ at $0$ with $n=1$ gives $|\cos\theta-1|\le\theta^2/2$, because $|\cos''|\le1$; hence $|e^{i\theta}-1|^2=2(1-\cos\theta)\le\theta^2$. Second, fix $y\in S$, $r\ge2a$, $n\in S^2$, and put $R:=|rn-y|$ and $h(s):=|rn-sy|$ for $s\in[0,1]$; then $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ with $h(0)=r$, $h(1)=R$, $h'(0)=-n\cdot y$, $h'(s)=-(rn-sy)\cdot y/h(s)$, $h''(s)=|y|^2/h(s)-((rn-sy)\cdot y)^2/h(s)^3$, so $|h''|\le2|y|^2/h(s)\le2a^2/(r-a)\le4a^2/r$ by $h(s)\ge r-a\ge r/2$; the Taylor bound at $0$ with $n=1$ gives $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le2a^2/r$, and then $|r/R-1|=|r-R|/R\le(a+2a^2/r)/(r/2)=2a/r+4a^2/r^2\le4a/r$ since $|r-R|\le|n\cdot y|+2a^2/r\le a+a=2a$, $R\ge r/2$, and $r\ge2a$ gives $4a^2/r^2\le2a/r$. Third, with $R$ as above, $\partial_rR=(r-n\cdot y)/R$ satisfies $|\partial_rR|\le1$ and $|\partial_rR-1|\le|R-r+n\cdot y|/R\le4a^2/r^2$, and the exact kernel derivatives give $\partial_rG_k(rn-y)=\partial_rR\,(ik-1/R)\,e^{ikR}/(4\pi R)$ and hence $|\partial_rG_k-ikG_k|\le(1/(4\pi R))\,[\,k|\partial_rR-1|+|\partial_rR|/R\,]\le2ka^2/(\pi r^3)+1/(\pi r^2)$.

[Fresnel substitution and estimates] Fix the planar observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$ with $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, and let $y\in S$ with transverse part $y_t$; put $d_0:=a+b$, $s:=|\xi-y_t|^2/z^2$, so that $0\le s\le\eta_0^2<1$ on the declared range. Decomposing the Euclidean norm by [F6], $R=|x-y|=z\sqrt{1+s}$, hence $1/R=(1/z)(1+s)^{-1/2}$ and the Fresnel replacements are $R_F:=z(1+s/2)$ and $1/z$. The Taylor bound of [F6] at $0$ with $n=1$ gives $|\sqrt{1+s}-1-s/2|\le s^2/8$, because $|(d^2/dt^2)\sqrt{1+t}|=|\!-\!\frac14(1+t)^{-3/2}|\le1/4$ on $[0,s]$; the Taylor bound with $n=0$ gives $|(1+s)^{-1/2}-1|\le s/2$, because $|(d/dt)(1+t)^{-1/2}|=\frac12(1+t)^{-3/2}\le1/2$. Consequently the phase error satisfies $k|R-R_F|=kz|\sqrt{1+s}-1-s/2|\le kd_0^4/(8z^3)$, and the relative amplitude error satisfies $|1-(1+s)^{-1/2}|\le s/2\le d_0^2/(2z^2)$, where $s\le d_0^2/z^2$ by $|\xi-y_t|\le d_0$.

[Period average equals the model intensity] Fix $x$ with $x_3>0$ and write $u=u(x)\in\mathbb C$; then $U(x,s)=\operatorname{Re}(ue^{-i\omega s})$, so [F4] applied with the complex number $u$ in both slots gives $\frac1T\int_0^TU(x,s)^2\,ds=\frac12|u|^2=I(x)$.

[Fraunhofer estimate at the closed radius] Fix $y\in S$, $r\ge2a$ and $n\in S^2$, and write $R=|rn-y|$. Using only the bounds of step 1.2 and the addition law of the exponential for $e^{ik(r-n\cdot y)}=e^{ikr}e^{-ikn\cdot y}$ from [F6], one has $\bigl|G_k(rn-y)-e^{ikr}e^{-ikn\cdot y}/(4\pi r)\bigr|=\bigl|e^{ikR}(r/R-1)+e^{ikR}-e^{ik(r-n\cdot y)}\bigr|/(4\pi r)\le(1/(4\pi r))\,[\,4a/r+k\cdot2a^2/r\,]\le(1/(\pi r))\,[\,a/r+ka^2/r\,]$, since $4/(4\pi)=1/\pi$ and $2/(4\pi)\le1/\pi$, and because the middle term was bounded by $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$ with $\theta:=k(R-r+n\cdot y)$ and $|\theta|\le2ka^2/r$. Integrating against $\alpha$ with the bound of [F3], applied to the bounded continuous function $y\mapsto G_k(rn-y)-e^{ikr}e^{-ikn\cdot y}/(4\pi r)$ on the compact support, gives $|u(rn)-e^{ikr}(4\pi r)^{-1}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}(\pi r)^{-1}[a/r+ka^2/r]$, uniformly in $n$; this is the displayed Fraunhofer estimate with a universal constant.

[Absolute field error of the Fresnel replacement] With the substitutions of step 1.3, for $y\in S$: $\bigl|G_k(x-y)-e^{ikR_F}/(4\pi z)\bigr|\le(1/(4\pi))\,|1/R-1/z|+(1/(4\pi z))\,|e^{ikR}-e^{ikR_F}|\le(1/(4\pi))\,d_0^2/(2z^3)+(1/(4\pi z))\,k\,d_0^4/(8z^3)=(1/(4\pi z))\,[\,d_0^2/(2z^2)+kd_0^4/(8z^3)\,]$, where the first summand used $|1/R-1/z|=(1/z)|(1+s)^{-1/2}-1|\le d_0^2/(2z^3)$ and the second used $|e^{ikR}-e^{ikR_F}|\le k|R-R_F|\le kd_0^4/(8z^3)$ from the phase estimate of step 1.3. Integrating against $\alpha$ with [F3] gives $|u(x)-u_{\rm Fresnel}(x)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}(4\pi z)^{-1}[d_0^2/(2z^2)+kd_0^4/(8z^3)]$, the displayed absolute field error with universal constants; the phase and relative amplitude errors of step 1.3 are those displayed in (b).

[Outgoing residual] With the third bound of step 1.2 and the same integration against the total variation [F3], $r|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\le r\int|\partial_rG_k(rn-y)-ikG_k(rn-y)|\,d|\alpha|(y)\le\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}\,[\,2ka^2/(\pi r^2)+1/(\pi r)\,]$, which is uniformly $O(\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}r^{-1})$ in direction; this and step 2.1 give clause (a).

[Intensity error transfer] Let $u_{\rm approx}$ satisfy $|u_{\rm approx}(x)-u(x)|\le\delta(x)$ at the point $x$. By the reverse triangle inequality of [F5], $\bigl||u_{\rm approx}|-|u|\bigr|\le|u_{\rm approx}-u|\le\delta$, and by $|z|^2=z\overline z$ and multiplicativity of the modulus [F5], $\bigl||u_{\rm approx}|^2-|u|^2\bigr|=\bigl||u_{\rm approx}|-|u|\bigr|\,(|u_{\rm approx}|+|u|)\le\delta(x)(|u(x)|+|u_{\rm approx}(x)|)$; multiplying by $\frac12$ and comparing with step 1.4 gives the first bound of (c). If additionally $u(x)\ne0$ and $|u_{\rm approx}-u|\le\epsilon(x)|u(x)|$, then $|u_{\rm approx}|\le(1+\epsilon(x))|u(x)|$, so the absolute intensity error is at most $\frac12\epsilon(x)|u(x)|\,(2+\epsilon(x))|u(x)|=\bigl(\epsilon(x)+\frac12\epsilon(x)^2\bigr)|u(x)|^2=(2\epsilon(x)+\epsilon(x)^2)I(x)$, which is the stated relative bound; applying these two estimates to the Fraunhofer and Fresnel field errors of steps 2.1, 3.1 and 2.2 gives the final sentence of (c) with no new approximation.

[Trace caveat, scope and choice accounting] The aperture distribution $\alpha$ is the adopted datum of [F1] and is not identified with the exact Maxwell boundary data on the screen; by [F2] assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, so no such identification or well-posedness is made. The construction never asserts that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations; it ignores polarization and aperture back-reaction, and it makes no measured-intensity, apparatus, sampling or empirical claim, only model comparisons of $I$ between observation points; this is clause (d). The only choice principle used is the Countable Choice carried by the two suppliers of [F2] and used in their trace and kernel interfaces; the period average of step 1.4 uses only the choice-free period-average lemma, and all other steps are explicit estimates and finite computations, so no further choice is invoked.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative to $\mu$** is the measure $$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$ whose measure property is supplied by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define $$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$ The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal. Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write $$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and $\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every** set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$ In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box $B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite parameters the value is already $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and $$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$ If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and $$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$ The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with $$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$ Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$ **Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything (the sign function); both witnesses are on the companion page. **No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form: the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for continuous integrands.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. For every real $x$, $$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$ Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.
For every real $x$, $$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$ Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). **The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then: 1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$. 2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$ 3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with $m, M$ real, then $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$ **Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is [[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] below. **Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives $\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when $u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then: 1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable; 2. and in that case $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$ 3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary. Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$ Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the form used everywhere below.

If $E\cap S=\varnothing$ then $R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E)=\varnothing$, so $\alpha$ is supported in $S$. For every countable Borel partition $\{E_m\}$ of $\mathbb R^3$, the defining values sum to $|A_0|\sum_m\lambda_2(R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E_m))=|A_0|\lambda_2(R)=4ab|A_0|$ by countable additivity and [F2]; taking the supremum over partitions gives $\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}=4ab|A_0|<+\infty$.

[Pairing identity] For a complex simple Borel function $s$ on $\mathbb R^3$ the defining sum of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]] gives $\int s\,d\alpha=A_0\int_R s\circ\jmath\,d\lambda_2$ because $s\circ\jmath$ is simple on $R$ and each level set is $R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E)$ for a level set $E$ of $s$. For an arbitrary bounded Borel $f$, approximate uniformly by finite simple functions and pass to the limit using the bound $|\int(f-s)\,d\alpha|\le\|f-s\|_\infty\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}$ of [F3]; hence $\int f\,d\alpha=A_0\int_Rf\circ\jmath\,d\lambda_2$ for every bounded Borel $f$ on $\mathbb R^3$.

[Fraunhofer amplitude] Fix $n\in S^2$ and put $f(y):=e^{-ikn\cdot y}$, which is continuous on the compact support; by step 2.1, $\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)=A_0\int_R e^{-ik(n_1y_1+n_2y_2)}\,d\lambda_2(y_1,y_2)$ because $y=\jmath(y_1,y_2)$ and $n\cdot y=n_1y_1+n_2y_2$ by [F5]. The integrand is continuous on the compact rectangle $R$, hence Riemann integrable, so the Lebesgue integral equals the Riemann double integral by [F4], and the Riemann double integral factors as the product of the one-dimensional integrals $\int_{-a}^ae^{-ikn_1y_1}dy_1$ and $\int_{-b}^be^{-ikn_2y_2}dy_2$ by [F4]. For $n_1\ne0$ the map $y_1\mapsto e^{-ikn_1y_1}/(-ikn_1)$ is an antiderivative with derivative $e^{-ikn_1y_1}$ by the chain, algebra and trigonometric derivative rules of [F5], so the second fundamental theorem gives $\int_{-a}^ae^{-ikn_1y_1}dy_1=(e^{-ikn_1a}-e^{ikn_1a})/(-ikn_1)=2\sin(ka\,n_1)/(kn_1)=2a\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)$; for $n_1=0$ the integral is $2a=2a\operatorname{sinc}0$ by the separate value of sinc. The second factor is analogous, giving the displayed identity $4abA_0\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)$ for every direction $n$.

[Fraunhofer intensity] For $r\ge2a'$ the support bound $|y|\le a'$ of [F2] puts the model in the regime of the Fraunhofer estimate of [F1] with aperture radius $a'$, so $u(rn)=e^{ikr}(4\pi r)^{-1}\cdot4abA_0\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)+R(rn)$ with $|R(rn)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}(\pi r)^{-1}[a'/r+k(a')^2/r]$ uniformly in direction by step 3.1. Taking moduli, $|u_{\rm F}(rn)|=\dfrac{ab|A_0|}{\pi r}\,|\!\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)|\,|\!\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)|$, so $I_{\rm F}(rn)=\frac12|u_{\rm F}(rn)|^2=\dfrac{a^2b^2|A_0|^2}{2\pi^2r^2}\operatorname{sinc}^2(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}^2(kb\,n_2)$, and the intensity-error transfer of [F1] bounds $\bigl|I(rn)-I_{\rm F}(rn)\bigr|$ by the Fraunhofer field error.

[Zeros of the pattern] By definition of sinc and the zero set of sine in [F6], $\operatorname{sinc}\xi=0$ exactly when $\xi\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$; since $k,a,b>0$ and the two factors multiply, $I_{\rm F}(rn)=0$ exactly when $ka\,n_1\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ or $kb\,n_2\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$.

[Global maxima] First, $|\sin x|\le|x|$ for every real $x$, with equality exactly at $x=0$: for $x>0$ choose $\delta:=\min\{x/3,\pi/6\}>0$; on $[\delta,2\delta]\subseteq[0,\pi/2]$ the cosine is positive and strictly decreasing, so $|\cos t|=\cos t\le\cos\delta<1$ there, while $|\cos t|\le1$ everywhere; the second fundamental theorem, the integral triangle bound and monotonicity of [F6] give $|\sin x|=\bigl|\int_0^x\cos t\,dt\bigr|\le\int_0^x|\cos t|\,dt\le(x-\delta)+\delta\cos\delta=x-\delta(1-\cos\delta)<x$, and for $x<0$ oddness of sine in [F6] gives $|\sin x|=|\sin(-x)|<|x|$, while $x=0$ gives equality. Hence $|\!\operatorname{sinc}\xi|\le1$ with equality exactly at $\xi=0$; since $k,a,b>0$, the modulus of the product in step 4.1 equals the prefactor exactly when $ka\,n_1=0$ and $kb\,n_2=0$, that is $n_1=n_2=0$, which on $S^2$ means $n=(0,0,\pm1)$; these two poles are therefore exactly the global maxima of the pattern on $S^2$, and the model's half-space $x_3>0$ forces $n_3>0$, leaving only the positive pole.

[Scope and choice accounting] The computation is exact inside the adopted scalar model: by [F1] it inherits the Fraunhofer and Fresnel error bounds rather than re-estimating them, it makes no measured-intensity, apparatus, sampling or calibration claim, and no polarization or screen-interaction content is introduced; only model comparisons of $I$ between observation points are read from it, which is clause (c). The only choice principle used is the Countable Choice carried by the parent theorem and by the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison and Fubini interfaces of [F4]; the remaining steps are explicit finite computations, so no further choice is made.
